name: Vacuum diode
description: Inside a vacuum tube. The left plate is a hot cathode: its right face emits electrons (blue dots), as many as its field pulls off. The right plate, the anode, is on your power supply. Set its voltage so that a current between 0.9 and 1.5 reaches the anode (averaged over $t = 10$ to $20$). The electrons in flight repel the ones behind them: this space charge chokes the current, which grows as $I \propto V^{3/2}$ (Child and Langmuir), faster than in proportion to the voltage. The potential map shows the space charge as a flat region in front of the cathode, where the field is pulled down to zero.

reality.represents: A planar vacuum diode: the Child–Langmuir law

remarks.line: Space charge from the electrons themselves
remarks.detail: Every electron in flight repels the others, and the charge it induces on the electrodes is solved at every step: the space-charge limit (Child and Langmuir) comes out of the simulation, not from a formula.
The current grows faster than the voltage: the space-charge law of every space-charge-limited diode.

The tube is the same all along its length: its electrodes are long prisms, its electrons long lines of charge, its currents per unit length. A real tube is a few centimetres long and has end effects; the textbooks' planar and coaxial laws assume this symmetry too.

The cathode gives off as many electrons as its field pulls off (the space-charge limit), released at rest. A real hot cathode emits them with thermal energies of about 0.1 eV, which lets a little current flow against a small retarding field and moves the potential's minimum slightly out from its face.
This cathode gives whatever the field pulls; a real one's temperature caps the current (Richardson's law: the Electron gun level).
